liverpool-retailers-and-sustainability-e.author: Ben Sillitoe
liverpool-retailers-and-sustainability-e.core: Posted in last 7 days Liverpool Retailers & Sustainability Experts - Circular Retail Scene Loads of things going on in my working world at the moment, events and content etc, but here's a little snapshot of some of the circular-thinking/planet-conscious retail businesses I spotted on a recent trip to #Liverpool. I've always loved the city and what it has to offer (up the Reds 🔴) but I'm considering a bit of a deepdive into the city's retail scene and its focus on sustainability. Drop me a line if you've got a contribution or some ideas of things to explore. Here are a few things I do know, for starters. For the last two years, Liverpool ONE has had a Mobile Segregation Unit (MSU), courtesy of The Green Block which aims to boost recycling rates at the shopping and leisure hub. The aim of the MSU deployment was to sort waste into 15 individual waste streams, making it easier to recycle more material. There's a digital waste tracking element to it all too. Didn't get to see that myself last week but, in terms of other sustainability/circularity plays, I did visit the colourful LUSH flagship in Church St, complete with its well marketed Bring it Back packaging recycling concept and mandate of "leaving the world lusher than we found it". It's the biggest Lush store in the world to boot. Sostrene Grene opened its doors in Liverpool's Bold St in October 2023, and continues to highlight strong environmental welfare credentials via in-store messaging and customer communication. Just along the way, there's also Resurrection Bold St Liverpool, a long-time go-to place for multiple partner fashion brands as well as a host of vintage, preloved, and upcycled gear. Bold Street is also home to one of only two Shared Earth UK Limited stores in the UK (the other one and original site is in York). Its roots are steeped in ethical trading and addressing social and environmental issues, and it was good to see the hustle and bustle inside. The site started offering customers the option to refill their own packaging (with shampoo, washing-up liquid etc) long before it became more widely popular for retailers to do so.

taxpayers-with-ato-automated-review-debt.core: Posted in last 7 days Taxpayers With ATO Automated Review Debt - Robodebt Concerns ATO's automated review reversed my deductions without a human looking at evidence. Robodebt lessons not learned? I'm looking to speak with a journalist about what I believe is an automated decision-making problem at the ATO, and one that could affect a lot of people before they even know about it. What happened to me: My 2025-26 return was lodged and assessed in July, refund paid. Today I noticed an unexplained debt oon my ATO account, labelled "Tax Office initiated amended tax return". No letter, no myGov message, no request for receipts or explanation. When I called, it took the ATO officer a long time to find any explanation. She eventually told me an automated review had decided my work-related expenses were too high for my industry, so the deductions were reversed. She said there is no other rationale. I keep detailed records: every item with its rationale and work-use %, reconciled to bank statements. I've lodged an objection and it will be fine in the end despite the pain of time and effort. My concern is everyone who won't notice the debt, or just pays it because they assume the ATO must be right. After Robodebt, automated decisions that create debts without a human reviewing evidence or giving the person a chance to respond should be ringing alarm bells. If you're a journalist covering this area, please DM me. And if this has happened to you too, comment below. It would help to know how widespread it is. The transaction was on 1 Nov so I suspect everyone else impacted will only have the transaction from the 1 Nov so may not have even noticed it.

central-victoria-farmers-and-richmond-te.author: Slade Beard
central-victoria-farmers-and-richmond-te.core: Posted in last 7 days Central Victoria Farmers & Richmond Tenants - 72-Hour Supplies In January, a bushfire went through our nine-hectare farm in Central Victoria. The house and sheds survived; the fencing, irrigation and our beehives didn’t. Ten months on, through a flood and a very long winter, we’re still rebuilding. It’s taught me that preparedness isn’t about the first 72 hours. It’s about the months after. But that experience is very different from life in a unit in Richmond, where there are neighbours on every side but nowhere to store 36 litres of water, and the taps may stop when the building’s pumps lose power. This week, governments from London to Tokyo told their citizens to keep at least three days of food, water and supplies at home. Here, The New Daily asked whether Australians should do the same. I’ve been advocating preparedness my whole life. I grew up in a community where it was simply how you lived, and I later ran workshops on it. My career in emergency management and national security has only reinforced it. So it’s fascinating to hear governments finally saying it out loud. But “72 hours of supplies” means something very different on our nine-hectare farm in Central Victoria than it does in a unit in Richmond. We have water tanks and space, but we’re on our own when the roads close in a fire. An apartment has neighbours on every side but nowhere to store 36 litres of water, and the taps may stop when the building’s pumps lose power. I’m planning a short series on what preparedness really looks like across those differences. Before I start, I’d like to hear from you: Where do you live, and what would worry you most if the power, water or phones stopped for three days? What have you already done to prepare, and what’s stopped you doing more? Your answers will shape what I write. The New Daily

adults-who-stayed-silent-regret-from-not.core: Posted in last 7 days Adults Who Stayed Silent - Regret From Not Speaking Up What is a moment in your life where you stayed completely silent and let the world make a major choice for you—just because you were too anxious to speak up? I'm a writer, and I've been thinking a lot about the terrifying inertia that takes over when the thing we actually want is standing directly in front of us. For a project I'm recording this weekend, I'm exploring the concept of personal passivity—those moments where we stand completely frozen, knowing exactly what we want, but out of fear of rejection or looking foolish, we say nothing and just let momentum carry us down a path we didn't actually choose. It's the strategy of a tumbleweed, letting life just happenaroundyou. I want to hear from other people who get this. What is a moment from your own life where your fear of making the wrong choice or causing a scene kept you completely silent? A relationship you slid into, a job opportunity you didn't show up for, or a boundary you never set? Looking back, what do you wish you had chosen instead? former-vcu-students-in-richmond-title-ix.core: Posted in last 7 days Former VCU Students in Richmond - Title IX & RPD Response Help: Title IX Hello everyone! I'll spare you all the details of my own experience, but I wanted to share a little background and hopefully connect with others who may have gone through something similar. When I was a student at VCU (I graduated in 2018), I reported the person who sexually assaulted me to the university's Title IX office. What followed was an incredibly frustrating and disheartening process. Getting even basic updates felt like pulling teeth, very little investigation took place (the witnesses I provided were never even contacted by the school), and the process dragged on until I graduated. At that point, I was told that because I was no longer a student, they could no longer proceed with my case. I spent a year on campus with my rapist and VCU did nothing about it. I made multiple attempts to address my concerns with the university at the time, but unfortunately got nowhere. Since then, I've spoken with other individuals who have described remarkably similar experiences, as well as other concerning issues with how their reports were handled. I'm currently working with a reporter to bring attention to these experiences, and I'm hoping to connect with others who may have stories of their own involving VCU's Title IX office or the Richmond Police Department (RPD). Whether your experience was similar to mine or entirely different, I would love to hear from you if you're comfortable sharing. This could mean speaking directly with the reporter, sharing your experience privately with me, or simply having a conversation about what happened. There is absolutely no pressure to participate in any way beyond what you're comfortable with. I also want to make it abundantly clear that anyone who reaches out will be treated with the utmost respect, kindness, compassion, and discretion. I understand firsthand how difficult it can be to revisit these experiences, let alone share them with a stranger. I will never ask anyone to disclose more than they're comfortable sharing, and I completely respect anyone's decision not to participate. My hope is that by bringing these experiences together, we can shed light on potential systemic issues, encourage meaningful accountability, and hopefully help prevent others from going through the same thing. Universities have a responsibility to protect their students, take reports seriously, and follow through. Survivors deserve more than silence, delays, and unanswered questions. If you're comfortable reaching out, my DMs are open. And if you don't have a personal experience to share but are willing to help this reach someone who might, I would sincerely appreciate you sharing this post. Thank you for reading. ❤️
